hints: Focus on what causes a small M+1 peak just one mass unit above the molecular ion in a mass spectrum.
Count the carbon atoms carefully from the ring plus the side chain to get the molecular formula of vitamin C.
Multiply the number of carbons by 1.1% to get the M+1 size relative to M, then take that fraction of the 7.0% M peak abundance.
walkthrough:
**Find the number of carbons in vitamin C**

Look closely at the structure. The five-membered lactone ring contains 4 carbons and 1 oxygen, and the side chain contains 2 more carbons.

That gives $6$ carbon atoms in total, so the formula is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_8\text{O}_6$ which matches $M_r = 176$.

**Recall why the M+1 peak appears**

The M+1 peak is mainly due to molecules containing one $^{13}\text{C}$ atom instead of $^{12}\text{C}$.

Natural abundance of $^{13}\text{C}$ is about 1.1% per carbon atom, so:
$$\text{M+1 as % of M} = \text{number of C} \times 1.1\%$$

**Calculate the abundance of the M+1 peak**

For 6 carbons:
$$\text{M+1 as % of M} = 6 \times 1.1\% = 6.6\%$$

The M peak itself is only 7.0% abundant, so:
$$\text{abundance of M+1} = 0.066 \times 7.0\% = 0.462\%$$

options.A: Correct. With 6 carbons, M+1 is 6.6% of the size of M. 6.6% of 7.0% is 0.462%. This correctly uses the $^{13}$C contribution.
options.B: Incorrect. This is the value for 7 carbons (7 x 1.1% x 7.0%). You get this if you miscount and add one extra carbon, perhaps by miscounting the ring atoms.
options.C: Incorrect. This is the value for 8 carbons (8 x 1.1% x 7.0%). You get this if you count oxygen atoms as carbons or seriously overcount the skeleton.
options.D: Incorrect. This is the value for 9 carbons (9 x 1.1% x 7.0%). You get this if you count every vertex and heteroatom in the diagram as carbon.
